section.title: Parables and the Calming of the Storm
section.sectionRationale: Mark gathers Jesus' kingdom parables into one great teaching day by the sea, the sower and its explanation, the lamp, the measure, the secretly growing seed, and the mustard seed, all unfolding the mystery of the kingdom. Then, at evening, He crosses the lake and stills a deadly storm with a word, so that His teaching about the hidden kingdom is sealed by a display of the Creator's own authority.
section.thesis: The kingdom of God comes hidden and small, like seed sown in varied soils and a mustard grain, growing by God's own power to a great harvest; and the King who teaches its mystery is the Lord of creation who rules wind and wave with a word, so the only fitting response is to hear, receive, and trust.
section.frameNote: Six beats: the parable of the sower; the purpose of parables; the sower explained; the lamp and the measure; the growing seed and the mustard seed; and the stilling of the storm.

units.label: The parable of the sower
units.note: a farmer went out to sow

verses.text: Once again Jesus began to teach beside the sea, and such a large crowd gathered around Him that He got into a boat and sat in it, while all the people crowded along the shore.
And He taught them many things in {{parabole|parables}}, and in His teaching He said,
“Listen! A farmer went out to sow his seed.
And as he was sowing, some seed fell along the path, and the birds came and devoured it.
Some fell on rocky ground, where it did not have much soil. It sprang up quickly because the soil was shallow.
But when the sun rose, the seedlings were scorched, and they withered because they had no root.
Other seed fell among thorns, which grew up and choked the seedlings, and they yielded no crop.
Still other seed fell on good soil, where it sprouted, grew up, and produced a crop, one bearing thirtyfold, another sixtyfold, and another a hundredfold.”
Then Jesus said, “He who has ears to hear, let him hear.”

units.label: The purpose of the parables
units.note: the mystery of the kingdom given to you

verses.text: As soon as Jesus was alone with the Twelve and those around Him, they asked Him about the parable.
He replied, “The {{mysterion|mystery}} of the kingdom of God has been given to you, but to those on the outside everything is expressed in parables,
so that, ‘they may be ever seeing but never perceiving, and ever hearing but never understanding; otherwise they might turn and be forgiven.’”
Then Jesus said to them, “Do you not understand this parable? Then how will you understand any of the parables?
The farmer sows the {{logos|word}}.
Some are like the seeds along the path, where the word is sown. As soon as they hear it, Satan comes and takes away the word that was sown in them.
Some are like the seeds sown on rocky ground. They hear the word and at once receive it with joy.
But they themselves have no root, and they remain for only a season. When trouble or persecution comes because of the word, they quickly fall away.
Others are like the seeds sown among the thorns. They hear the word,
but the worries of this life, the deceitfulness of wealth, and the desire for other things come in and choke the word, and it becomes unfruitful.
Still others are like the seeds sown on good soil. They hear the word, receive it, and produce a crop, thirtyfold, sixtyfold, or a hundredfold.”

units.label: The lamp and the measure
units.note: nothing hidden that will not be disclosed

verses.text: Jesus also said to them, “Does anyone bring in a lamp to put it under a basket or under a bed? Doesn’t he set it on a stand?
For there is nothing hidden that will not be disclosed, and nothing concealed that will not be brought to light.
If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear.”
He went on to say, “Pay attention to what you hear. With the measure you use, it will be measured to you, and even more will be added to you.
For whoever has will be given more. But whoever does not have, even what he has will be taken away from him.”

units.label: The growing seed and the mustard seed
units.note: the kingdom grows by God's own power

verses.text: Jesus also said, “The kingdom of God is like a man who scatters seed on the ground.
Night and day he sleeps and wakes, and the seed sprouts and grows, though he knows not how.
All by itself the earth produces a crop, first the stalk, then the head, then grain that ripens within.
And as soon as the grain is ripe, he swings the sickle, because the harvest has come.”
Then He asked, “To what can we compare the kingdom of God? With what parable shall we present it?
It is like a mustard seed, which is the smallest of all seeds sown upon the earth.
But after it is planted, it grows to be the largest of all garden plants and puts forth great branches, so that the birds of the air nest in its shade.”
With many such parables Jesus spoke the word to them, to the extent that they could understand.
He did not tell them anything without using a parable. But privately He explained everything to His own disciples.

units.label: The stilling of the storm
units.note: who is this, that even wind and sea obey Him

verses.text: When that evening came, He said to His disciples, “Let us cross to the other side.”
After they had dismissed the crowd, they took Jesus with them, since He was already in the boat. And there were other boats with Him.
Soon a violent windstorm came up, and the waves were breaking over the boat, so that it was being swamped.
But Jesus was in the stern, sleeping on the cushion. So they woke Him and said, “Teacher, don’t You care that we are perishing?”
Then Jesus got up and {{epitimao|rebuked}} the wind and the sea. “Silence!” He commanded. “Be still!” And the wind died down, and it was perfectly calm.
“Why are you so afraid?” He asked. “Do you still have no {{pistis|faith}}?”
Overwhelmed with fear, they asked one another, “Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?”

parabole.gloss: A parable, a comparison or story laid alongside a truth to reveal it. Jesus' parables both disclose the kingdom to those who hear with faith and veil it from the hard-hearted, so that the same story enlightens some and hardens others.

mysterion.gloss: A mystery, a secret once hidden and now revealed by God. The mystery of the kingdom is that God's reign arrives not in overwhelming glory but hidden and small, in the person of Jesus and the sowing of His word, to be grasped only by those to whom it is given.

logos.gloss: Word, message. In the parable the seed is the word, the gospel of the kingdom. Its fruitfulness depends not on the sower or the seed but on the soil, the heart that hears; the same word meets hardness, shallowness, distraction, and fruitful reception.

epitimao.gloss: To rebuke, censure, command with authority. Jesus rebukes the wind and sea with the same authoritative word He uses on demons, treating the raging chaos as something to be silenced. Only the Creator can command the sea; His rebuke reveals who He is.

pistis.gloss: Faith, trust, reliance. Jesus asks the terrified disciples why they still have no faith. Faith here is not the absence of danger but trust in the One who is present in the boat, the Lord of the storm, even when He seems asleep to our cries.

basic.context: Jesus teaches a crowd from a boat, telling the parable of the sower: seed falls on a path, on rocky ground, among thorns, and on good soil, with only the last bearing a great crop. Privately He explains that the seed is God's word and the soils are kinds of hearers. He adds sayings about a lamp not meant to be hidden, and about the kingdom growing secretly like scattered seed and spreading like a tiny mustard seed into a great plant. Then, that evening, a fierce storm nearly sinks the boat while Jesus sleeps. The terrified disciples wake Him, and He stills the wind and sea with a word, leaving them awestruck: who is this?
basic.hermeneutics: The parables reveal the nature of the kingdom: it comes hidden and small, spreads by God's power, and calls for a hearing that truly receives. The parable of the sower is a key to the rest, warning us to examine what kind of soil our hearts are. The storm scene is not a separate topic but the seal on the teaching: the One whose word is the kingdom's seed is the Lord whose word commands creation.
basic.originalLanguages: Jesus teaches in parabole, parables, that reveal and conceal. To the disciples is given the mysterion, the mystery, of the kingdom. The seed is the logos, the word. On the lake He epitimao, rebukes, the wind and sea as He would a demon, and asks the disciples why they have no pistis, faith.
basic.typology: The stilling of the storm echoes the God of the Psalms who rules the raging sea and stills its waves. Jesus doing what only the LORD can do reveals Him as God with us. The harvest imagery draws on the prophets' picture of God's final ingathering.
basic.christ: Jesus is the sower of the word, the teacher of the kingdom's mystery, and the Lord of creation who commands wind and wave. The disciples' question, who is this, is the question the whole Gospel answers: He is the Son of God.
basic.god: God's kingdom advances by God's own power, growing while the farmer sleeps. The same God who rules the sea in the Psalms now stands in the boat. The word God sows will bear fruit and reach a great harvest despite every resistance.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 6 lies behind the parable's purpose. Psalm 107 shows the LORD stilling the storm. Joel 3 and Revelation 14 picture the final harvest.
basic.oneStory: God's reign, long promised, arrives in Jesus not with instant overwhelming glory but hidden like a seed, sown in His word and growing by His power toward a sure harvest. And the King who plants that seed is the Creator Himself, who silences the chaos of the sea with a word, assuring His people that the One in the boat with them holds all things in His hands.

context.literary:
Mark 4 is the longest block of Jesus' teaching in the first half of the Gospel, and it is organised around one command repeated like a drumbeat: listen. It opens with 'Listen!' in verse 3, and the verb 'to hear' keeps returning in verses 9, 12, 15, 16, 18, 20, 23, 24 and 33. The chapter is a lesson in hearing, and the way it is built teaches the lesson. The first parable is given to the crowd, 4:1-9, its explanation to the insiders, 4:10-20, and then comes a string of shorter parable sayings, lamp, measure, growing seed and mustard seed, 4:21-32, closed by the summary at verses 33 and 34.

The stilling of the storm, 4:35-41, is not an afterthought. It is the same lesson turned into an event. The chapter began with a crowd on the shore and Jesus in a boat teaching, and it ends with Jesus in a boat on the sea doing. The word of the sower, which 'the farmer sows,' becomes the word that silences the wind. Notice how Mark marks this joining: the boat of verse 1 returns in verse 36, where they take Him 'just as He was,' as the Greek has it, and the evening that closes a day of teaching opens a night of terror.

Several devices hold the chapter together. There are pairs of parables, one about a hidden power and growth that is secret, one about small beginnings and a large end. The growth parables share the theme that results come without the sower's control, 4:27. The saying of verse 22 sits in the middle as a hinge: what is hidden is hidden in order to be revealed. And the sowing parable is a kind of key. 'Do you not understand this parable? Then how will you understand any of the parables?' makes the sower the pattern for how all the rest are to be read.

Finally, the chapter sets its audience in three rings: the crowd, the Twelve and others around Him, and 'those on the outside,' as verse 11 has it. The Greek there repeats the word for 'outside' that Mark used in 3:31-32 for the family standing at the door. In both places the question is who stays outside and who comes in to sit near Him.
context.historical:
The farmer in the first parable is no figure of fantasy. In first-century Galilee seed was commonly scattered by hand over the ground and then ploughed in. That is why seed lands on a path, because the field was crossed by well-worn tracks, on stony ground, because limestone lies close under much of the thin Galilean soil, and among thorns, because the roots of last year's weeds survive in the earth. Jesus is describing a normal sowing, with its normal losses. What is not normal is the harvest, thirty, sixty, a hundredfold, far above what a good field might give. Genesis 26:12 records it as a sign of special blessing when Isaac reaped a hundredfold in a single year. The listeners were meant to hear that the loss is ordinary and the harvest is extraordinary.

The mustard plant was a familiar one. A mustard seed is tiny, and Jesus calls it 'the smallest of all seeds sown upon the earth,' a popular way of speaking about something very small, as in Matthew 17:20. The mature plant is a large shrub, not a tree, which makes the image of birds nesting in its shade a gentle joke, since the Old Testament pictures the kingdom as a great cedar or tree, Ezekiel 17:22-24 and Daniel 4:10-12. Jesus is deliberately choosing something humbler.

The Sea of Galilee lies well below sea level, ringed by hills and cut by ravines, and cold air sweeping down can whip the surface into a violent storm in a short time. Fishermen like Peter, Andrew, James and John would have known this well, which gives weight to Mark's picture of experienced sailors afraid for their lives. The boat was a working vessel, with a stern where a cushion or pad could be put for a helmsman or passenger to sit on.

For Israelites, the sea was more than weather. It was a place of chaos and danger, the haunt of sea monsters in poetry, Psalm 74:13-14, and the only one who could subdue it was God, Job 38:8-11 and Psalm 89:9. A crossing at night in a squall was a picture of being at the mercy of forces no one can handle. And the 'other side' toward which Jesus is heading is Gentile country, the region of the Gerasenes in 5:1, so the storm lies across the path into a land that was outside Israel's pale.
context.canonical:
The parable of the sower stands where Isaiah's commission stands. In Isaiah 6:9-10 the prophet is told to speak to a people who will go on hearing without understanding. Mark 4:12 quotes that text, and Jesus applies it to the response His own teaching meets. The pattern had a long history. Moses told Israel that the LORD had not yet given them a mind to understand or eyes to see, Deuteronomy 29:2-4, Jeremiah called them a people with eyes that do not see, Jeremiah 5:21, and Jesus will say the same of His own disciples, Mark 8:17-18. Matthew 13:13-15 and John 12:37-41 both draw on Isaiah 6, as does Acts 28:25-28, the last words of Luke's story.

The seed that is the word echoes Isaiah 55:10-11, where God's word goes out like rain and snow, does not return empty, and accomplishes what He pleases. The New Testament picks up the seed as a picture of the word: 1 Peter 1:23 speaks of being born again of imperishable seed, the living word of God, and James 1:21 of the implanted word that can save.

The growing seed ends in a harvest picture that reaches back to Joel 3:13, 'Swing the sickle, for the harvest is ripe,' where harvest stands for the day of God's judgment. Mark 4:29 borrows that language. The same image returns in Revelation 14:14-16. The mustard shrub and its birds invoke the tree of Ezekiel 17:23, where God plants a sprig that will become a majestic cedar sheltering birds of every kind, and the tree of Daniel 4:12, where the birds nest in the branches. Both have the nations in view.

The storm belongs with the many places where God rules the sea: Job 38:8-11, Psalm 65:7, Psalm 89:9 and especially Psalm 107:23-30, where sailors cry out in a storm and the LORD calms it. Jonah 1 offers a contrasting story, a prophet asleep in a boat in a storm, who must be thrown overboard to quiet it. Jesus too sleeps in the storm, but He calms it Himself, and He is the one who will be cast into the depths of death for others. The New Testament's continued witness to Jesus as the Creator, Colossians 1:16-17 and Hebrews 1:3, makes sense of the scene.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Mark wrote this chapter for a church that was meeting resistance. Some of its hearers would have been shocked that the message about Jesus did not win everyone. The sower answers that discouragement directly. Opposition, shallowness and distraction are expected, and they do not mean that the seed is bad or the sower has failed. At the same time Mark challenges every reader: which of these soils am I? The chapter is not content to let readers be spectators of other people's hearing.

Mark also wants his readers to see that the kingdom does not look like what most people hoped. A conquering kingdom would arrive with force. This one arrives as seed. It looks small, it grows by a power beyond human effort, and it comes to a harvest only God can time. The people who were impatient for Messiah to overthrow Rome needed this parable, and so did the discouraged disciples. The man who sleeps and wakes while the seed grows is not lazy, and the point is not that work is unimportant. It is that the growth is not his doing, and that he can rest in that.

The storm tells Mark's readers who is in the boat. Early believers were often afraid, in danger, and tempted to think Jesus did not care. The disciples' cry, 'don't You care that we are perishing?', is every believer's cry, and Mark's answer is that the one asleep in the stern is the Lord of the sea. The chapter closes with a question, 'Who is this?', and Mark means his readers to carry it forward through the rest of the Gospel until Peter and then a centurion answer it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The parables describe how the kingdom works and the explanation of the sower describes kinds of hearing. They are not commands about technique. The chapter does not instruct anyone to sow in a particular way or to sort people into categories. Believers are not told to decide which of their neighbours is rocky ground and stop speaking to them. The sower in the story scatters seed widely and without calculation, and that is itself a picture of how generous the word is meant to be.

The challenge to examine the heart is prescriptive in the true sense: 'Pay attention to what you hear,' verse 24, is an instruction. We are told to take care how we listen, and the explanation names the specific dangers, trouble, worry, wealth and desire, that threaten the fruit.

The storm is a record of what happened once, not a promise that every storm will end the moment we pray. Nothing in it says that faithful people will be spared shipwreck. Paul was shipwrecked three times, 2 Corinthians 11:25. What does carry forward is the character of the One in the boat and His question: why are you so afraid? The passage invites trust in Him, not a formula for stilling the weather.

debates.question: Do the parables reveal the kingdom or conceal it?

views.label: They do both, depending on the hearer
views.case: Verses 11 and 12 say the mystery is given to the inner circle while those outside meet it only in parables, as Isaiah 6 foretold. The same story enlightens a receptive hearer and leaves a closed one in the dark. Mark's use of the word 'so that' in verse 12 is purposeful, so the concealing is part of God's design.

views.label: They invite, and judge those who refuse
views.case: The parables draw people in with ordinary images and give the willing a reason to ask, as the disciples do in verse 10. The ones who walk away are left in the blindness they chose. Matthew 13:13 gives the reason as 'because,' not 'so that,' and some think Mark's purpose clause carries the same sense, a judgment on those already refusing.

views.label: A Mark-wide pattern of secrecy
views.case: Mark's Gospel has a theme of hiddenness, with commands to be silent, 1:34 and 3:12, and a gradual unveiling. On this reading the parables belong to that pattern: the kingdom has to be seen with the eyes of faith, and the full truth cannot be grasped until the cross and the resurrection.

debates.bearing: All three agree that response is decisive and that the invitation is real. The repeated 'He who has ears to hear, let him hear,' shows that the veiling is never a locked door to the humble seeker.

debates.question: What is the main point of the parable of the sower?

views.label: A warning to examine how we hear
views.case: The four soils press every hearer to ask what kind of ground their heart is, since the same seed meets hardness, shallowness, distraction and good reception. Mark's explanation spends most of its words on the dangers, which points toward a call to examine ourselves.

views.label: An assurance that the kingdom will bear fruit despite loss
views.case: Three of four soils fail, yet the fourth yields far above any ordinary harvest. For disciples facing opposition and a small beginning, the parable says that the word will accomplish its purpose, as Isaiah 55:10-11 promised.

views.label: An explanation of why Jesus is rejected
views.case: Set after the verdicts of chapter 3, the parable explains why many hear Jesus and do not follow. The failure of the word to take root in some is not a sign that Jesus is wrong but exactly what the sower expects.

debates.bearing: The readings do not compete. The parable comforts the discouraged sower, warns the hearer, and explains the mixed response Jesus meets, which is why Jesus makes it the key to every other parable.

debates.question: Are the rocky ground and thorny soil true believers who lose their salvation?

views.label: They were never truly saved
views.case: The seed on rock has 'no root,' verse 17, and the thorn hearers produce no crop, verse 19. Reformed readers hold that real faith bears fruit and endures, citing John 15:6 and 1 John 2:19, so these hearers only looked as though they believed.

views.label: They are real believers who fall away
views.case: Arminian readers point to the joyful reception in verse 16 and to warnings such as Hebrews 6:4-6 and 10:26-29, and argue that the passage describes people who really did receive the word and then abandoned it.

views.label: The parable does not answer the question
views.case: Jesus is describing responses to the word, not drawing the line of eternal security. He is concerned with what yields fruit. The category of 'enduring' fruit is the test, and the text leaves the inner state of the rocky hearer unsettled.

debates.bearing: Whatever one concludes about eternal security, the pastoral thrust is plain: do not trust a quick warm response, and do not let worry and wealth quietly choke a living word.

study.originalLanguages:
The word for the stories themselves is parabole, and the sense behind it is the Hebrew mashal, which covers proverb, riddle, comparison and dark saying alike. That breadth matters because in verse 11 Jesus says to those outside 'everything is expressed in parables,' and the word there can lean toward riddle, something that has to be unlocked. In Mark 3:23 Jesus had already called His defence against the scribes 'parables,' and in Mark 7:17 the disciples again ask for an explanation of a parable. So a parable in Mark is not a simple illustration. It is a figure that demands a hearer.

The Greek of verse 12 deserves slow reading. It begins with hina, 'so that,' and ends with mepote, 'otherwise,' or 'lest.' The grammar is purposive, which is why the saying is so hard. Matthew's parallel, Matthew 13:13, uses hoti, 'because,' which softens it. Mark also quotes Isaiah 6:9-10 freely, ending with 'and be forgiven,' where the Hebrew has 'be healed,' a reading that matches the Aramaic paraphrase of Isaiah used in the synagogues. The surprising finish, forgiveness rather than healing, ties the passage to Mark's interest in forgiving sin, as in 2:5-10.

The word 'mystery' in verse 11 is mysterion, in the singular. Mark has one mystery, not many, and it is the kingdom itself, God's reign breaking in through a Person. In Paul the same word comes to mean a plan hidden for ages and now disclosed, Romans 16:25-26 and Colossians 1:26-27. Here it means that the kingdom has been 'given' to the disciples, a passive form that points to God as the giver, in the same sense that He gave the seed.

Verse 17 has a revealing verb. The rocky hearers 'fall away,' which is the verb skandalizo, to be tripped up or made to stumble. It is the verb Mark uses for the offence the people of Nazareth take at Jesus in 6:3. They have no root, so when trouble comes because of the word, they take offence. The same Greek word covers the failure of the shallow soil and the failure of the hometown crowd.

Verse 19 lists three enemies: the worries of this age, merimnai, the deceitfulness of wealth, apate, and the desire for other things, epithymiai. The word for deceit is the word for something that misleads by promising satisfaction it cannot give. The thorns are not wicked in themselves. They are good things growing too thick.

The seed that 'grows by itself' in verse 28 uses the word automate, from which English takes 'automatic.' The earth produces a crop 'by itself,' and the word does not occur anywhere else in the four Gospels. It marks the sower's lack of control: he sleeps and rises, and the growth goes on. The next phrase, 'the stalk, then the head, then the full grain,' gives the growth three stages, and the verb for the harvest, 'the harvest has come,' echoes the sickle language of Joel 3:13.

Finally, the storm. Verse 39 says Jesus 'rebuked' the wind, epitimao, the verb Mark uses for His commands to demons in 1:25 and 3:12. The next word, 'Be still,' is the verb phimoo, literally 'be muzzled,' used in 1:25 for the demon in the synagogue, 'Be silent.' Jesus speaks to the sea as to a hostile power. And Mark pairs three 'greats': a 'great' squall, lailaps megale, in verse 37, a 'great' calm, galene megale, in verse 39, and in verse 41 a 'great fear,' phobon megan, so that the disciples' terror of the storm gives way to a greater terror of the one who stilled it. Jonah's sailors have the same experience in Jonah 1:16, where after the sea grows calm they fear the LORD greatly.

typology.type: The sower and the seed, the word of God going out
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah 55:10-11 pictures God's word going out like rain and snow and accomplishing His purpose. Jesus is the sower who scatters that word in person, and the parable explains why it meets mixed ground. Escalation comes in John 1:14, where the Word becomes flesh, and in 1 Peter 1:23, where believers are born of the imperishable seed of the word. The picture falls short in one respect: the soils in the parable seem fixed, while the New Testament promises that God can break up hard ground and give a heart of flesh, Ezekiel 36:26.

typology.type: The mustard shrub and the great tree of the nations
typology.fulfillment: The Old Testament pictures God's kingdom as a tree that shelters the nations, a cedar planted by God on the heights of Israel in Ezekiel 17:22-24, and an enormous tree in Nebuchadnezzar's dream in Daniel 4:10-12. Jesus takes the image and shrinks the start: the kingdom begins as a tiny seed and becomes a large plant where birds shelter. The story of Acts shows this happening, from a handful of disciples to a church that includes every nation, and Revelation 7:9 sees the full harvest. The plant is not a tree, so the picture also says the kingdom will be humbler than anyone expected.

typology.type: The sea as the realm of chaos and the Lord who rules it
typology.fulfillment: In Israel's poetry God subdues the sea, Psalm 89:9, and rescues sailors from storms, Psalm 107:23-30. The sea is also where Israel was saved at the Red Sea, Exodus 14:21-22. In the stilling of the storm Jesus does what the Psalms say only God does, and Mark's question, who is this, calls for the answer that He is the one who rules the sea. This reaches its end in the new creation, where 'there was no longer any sea,' Revelation 21:1. The sea itself is not evil, so the picture is of a threat that is finally removed, not a creature that is destroyed.

Jonah slept in the hold while a great wind threatened the ship, Jonah 1:4-6, and the sailors woke him and begged him to call on his God. Jesus too sleeps in a boat in a storm, and the disciples wake Him. The two scenes line up deliberately. Jesus later says that no sign will be given except the sign of Jonah, Matthew 12:39-41. The escalation is that Jonah was the cause of the storm and was thrown into the sea to end it, while Jesus is without fault and ends the storm with a word. The correspondence breaks down because Jonah fled from God's presence, while Jesus is God's presence in the boat.

study.christ:
This chapter leads to Christ in two directions that meet in the last verse. The first half presents Him as the sower. The word that He sows is His own, and the harvest He expects is His own. Mark shows Jesus speaking with a settled authority, 'Listen!', and what He sows is the word about the arrival of the kingdom, which is itself a word about Him. The first chapter of Mark summarised His message as 'the kingdom of God is near,' Mark 1:15, and the parable explains what happens when that message is preached. When we read later in Acts that the word grew and multiplied, Acts 6:7 and 12:24, we are watching the seed of the parable bear its fruit.

The second half presents Him as Lord of creation. Nothing in the parables would lead a reader to expect it. A teacher of parables stands up in a boat and speaks to a storm with the same words He used to silence demons. The Psalms never ask anyone but God to hush the waves, and the disciples' question, 'Who is this?', is a fair one. The people who first answered it did not say prophet or teacher. Colossians says that all things were created through Him and hold together in Him, Colossians 1:16-17, and Hebrews says He 'upholds all things by the word of His power,' Hebrews 1:3. The wind and sea are not obeying a magician, but their Maker.

The sleeping Jesus is also a window onto His humanity. The Lord of the sea is tired, so tired that wave after wave breaking into the boat does not wake Him. He is fully God and fully man. We are shown real weariness alongside real authority, and Mark does not try to resolve the tension. He is the one who can sleep because He trusts the Father, as Psalm 4:8 says of the righteous, and the one who can rise and rule because He is the Son.

The chapter also points to the cross, because the parable of the sower is itself about how the word is received. The word will be met with the thorns of worry and the rocky ground of persecution, and the one who sows it will meet the same, being rejected and killed. The saying that nothing hidden will fail to be disclosed finds its fullest answer there. The cross and the resurrection are when what has been kept hidden is finally brought into the open, which is why the disciples' understanding will not be complete until then.

Another link is the harvest. The man 'swings the sickle' when the grain is ripe. In the prophets the harvest is the day of God, and Jesus takes that language for the end, when the Son of Man gathers His own, Mark 13:27. The sower of chapter 4 is the harvester of the end of the age.

As ever, restraint is wise. The four soils are not four stages of Christ's life, and the cushion in the stern is not a hidden symbol. The links above rest on what the Gospel and the rest of the New Testament say outright.
study.god:
The most striking thing this chapter says about God is how He prefers to work: quietly, patiently, and by a power that does not depend on the human worker. The farmer in the growing seed parable sleeps and wakes while the seed grows, 'he knows not how.' God's kingdom is not built by human energy. That is a comfort to the discouraged, and it is also a rebuke to anyone who thinks they can force the growth or who gives up when they cannot see it. The harvest belongs to God, and so does its timing.

He is a God who speaks and is heard in spite of resistance. The sower scatters his seed on bad ground as well as good, and that picture shows divine generosity: God sends His word to path, rock and thorn alike. He does not hold back from giving the word to those who may not receive it. At the same time, the chapter takes seriously that God is the one who gives understanding. 'The mystery of the kingdom of God has been given to you,' and the passive voice points to Him. Understanding is a gift. Deuteronomy 29:4 says the LORD had not yet given Israel a mind to understand, and Hosea 6:3 and Jeremiah 31:33-34 look to the day when He would. The same God who hides is the God who reveals.

He is a God who judges by hardening those who harden themselves. Isaiah 6 describes a hardening that is both a judgment and an expression of what people have already become. The passage keeps the human responsibility intact: the soils differ, the hearers are told to listen, and no one is excused. Yet the passage also does not let the matter rest on human decision alone. We are left with a tension that Scripture often leaves open, and we are right to hold both truths.

He is Lord over nature. Job 38 pictures God shutting the sea behind doors and saying 'You may come this far, but no farther.' Psalm 107 shows Him calming a storm to a whisper. In Mark 4 this very rule is exercised by Jesus. So the passage shapes the doctrine of God by placing the Son on the side of the Creator. The Father's rule over the sea is the Son's rule too.

God is also near in the storm. The disciples feared that Jesus did not care. The Psalms voice the same cry, 'Wake up, O Lord! Why are You sleeping?' Psalm 44:23. The passage does not deny the feeling. It answers it by showing that the One who seemed absent was in the boat all along, and that He was able to act the moment He was asked. His rebuke is not for crying out. It is for fear that forgot who was in the boat.

For worship, this means that we praise a God who gives the word freely, who gives understanding as a gift, who rules the wind and the sea, and who is with us in the boat. The right response is not control but trust: to listen well, to let the word take root, and to keep our eyes on the One who sleeps in the stern and rules the storm.

crossReferences.note: Isaiah is commissioned to speak to a people who will hear without understanding. Mark 4:12 quotes it to explain why parables draw mixed responses. It frames the teaching as part of a long pattern in which God's word hardens those who have already turned from it.

God's word goes out like rain and snow, giving seed to the sower, and does not return empty. The sower's parable stands on this promise: despite the losses on path, rock and thorn, the word will prosper where God sends it.

Isaac sowed in the land and reaped a hundredfold in one year, and the LORD blessed him. The hundredfold in Mark 4:8 recalls the highest yield in Scripture, a sign of special blessing, showing that the good soil's harvest is beyond all ordinary expectation.

'Swing the sickle, for the harvest is ripe.' In Joel the harvest means the judgment of the nations. Mark 4:29 takes the sickle language from this verse and applies it to the kingdom, so that the quiet growth ends in the day of God.

God plants a sprig on the mountain heights of Israel and it becomes a majestic cedar where birds of every kind nest. The mustard plant of Mark 4:32 plays on the same picture, with a humbler plant and a kingdom that shelters people from every nation.

Nebuchadnezzar dreams of a great tree that feeds every creature and gives birds a place to nest in its branches. Mark's mustard shrub borrows the birds and the shelter, and the contrast between a great empire's tree and a small garden plant is part of Jesus' point.

Sailors in a storm cry out to the LORD and He brings them out of distress, calming the storm to a whisper. The disciples' cry and Jesus' word in Mark 4:35-41 are the New Testament form of this psalm, with Jesus doing what the LORD does.

A great wind, a ship about to break apart, a sleeping prophet in the hold and frightened sailors. Mark's storm echoes Jonah's, but Jesus is not the cause of the storm and is not thrown overboard. He is the One who stills it.

God asks Job who shut the sea behind doors and set its limits. Only the Creator holds the sea to its boundary. When Jesus speaks to the sea in Mark 4:39 and it obeys, the passage claims the authority that Job 38 reserves for God alone.

Jesus asks the disciples whether they have eyes and do not see, ears and do not hear, using the language of Isaiah 6 and Jeremiah 5:21. The disciples are not immune from the problem of chapter 4, and Mark shows that the hearing he calls for is a lifelong struggle.

Matthew's version of the sower adds 'because' where Mark has 'so that' in explaining the parables, and adds that the hearers 'understand' the word in the good soil. Reading both helps to see the same teaching from two angles.

All things were created through Him and for Him, and in Him all things hold together. This is the New Testament's answer to the disciples' question in Mark 4:41. The wind and sea obey because they are His own creatures.

study.oneStory:
Genesis opens with the Spirit hovering over the waters and God's word bringing order out of the deep. The sea in Scripture stands for what is not yet ordered, and it is God's word that sets its boundary, Job 38:8-11. By the time of Mark 4, much of that order has been undone. The world is subject to futility, Romans 8:20, and the sea can take a boat full of fishermen. The stilling of the storm is the creating word spoken again into disorder, and this time it is heard from the lips of a man in the boat.

The sower belongs to the same story from the other end. From the beginning, God has spoken and creation has answered, 'and there was light.' Since the fall humans have heard and not answered. Israel's story is a long run of hearing without hearing, from Moses' complaint in Deuteronomy 29 to Isaiah's commission, and the prophets keep asking whether the word will bear fruit among a people with closed ears. Jesus stands in that line and, in the parable, tells why. Yet He also tells how it will end: the word does bear a harvest, and in the end it bears an astonishing one.

The kingdom's hidden, small beginning answers the question every discouraged believer asks, why does God's rule look so slight? The prophets spoke of a day when God would reign, and Israel pictured an overpowering arrival. Mark's answer is that God's reign is already here, planted like seed, to be completed at the harvest. The mustard plant becomes a home for the nations, which carries forward the promise to Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him, Genesis 12:3.

The chapter also faces forward to the cross. The seed must go into the ground to bear fruit, as Jesus will later say, John 12:24, and the lamp that is not hidden is lit by a death and resurrection that reveal what was hidden. The Gospel keeps asking 'Who is this?' until the centurion answers beneath the cross.

The new creation completes both strands. The word is fully received: 'they will all know Me, from the least of them to the greatest,' Jeremiah 31:34, and the people who hear are the people who see, Revelation 22:4. The sea that frightened the disciples is gone: 'there was no longer any sea,' Revelation 21:1. And the harvest is gathered. The man who slept in the stern becomes the One who sits on the throne and wipes every tear, Revelation 21:4, and the fear that gripped the boat gives way to a people who are at home with their King.

quiz.q: In the parable of the sower, what determines whether the seed bears fruit?

options.text: The condition of the soil, that is, the kind of heart that hears the word.
options.note: Jesus explains the soils as different hearers; fruitfulness depends on how the word is received, Mark 4:14-20.

options.text: The skill and effort of the farmer who sows.
options.note: The same seed is sown everywhere; the parable's focus is the soil, not the sower's skill.

options.text: The quality of the seed being different in each case.
options.note: The seed, the word, is the same; it is the soil that varies.

options.text: Pure chance, with no meaning to the outcomes.
options.note: The outcomes are deliberately explained by the state of each hearer's heart.

quiz.q: Why does Jesus teach the crowds in parables?

options.text: They reveal the mystery of the kingdom to those given to understand while leaving the hard-hearted seeing but not perceiving.
options.note: Mark 4:11-12 quotes Isaiah 6; parables both reveal and, in judgment, conceal.

options.text: Because stories are simply easier for crowds to remember.
options.note: Parables are memorable, but Jesus states a deeper purpose of revealing and concealing the kingdom.

options.text: To hide the truth entirely so no one could be saved.
options.note: They do veil the truth from the hard-hearted, but the repeated call to hear shows they also graciously invite.

options.text: Because He had no clear teaching to give plainly.
options.note: Jesus explained everything privately to His disciples; the parables were purposeful, not vague.

quiz.q: What do the growing seed and mustard seed parables teach about the kingdom?

options.text: It grows by God's own power from small, hidden beginnings to a great harvest and a vast reach.
options.note: Mark 4:26-32 shows the seed growing on its own and the mustard seed becoming the largest plant.

options.text: It grows steadily larger over time.
options.note: True in part, but it misses that the growth is God's own doing and starts from hidden smallness.

options.text: It depends mainly on human effort to expand.
options.note: The seed grows though the man sleeps and knows not how; the emphasis is God's power, not human effort.

options.text: It will always remain small and unnoticed.
options.note: The mustard seed becomes the largest plant; the kingdom's reach becomes great.

quiz.q: What does Jesus' stilling of the storm reveal about Him?

options.text: That He is the Lord of creation, doing what the Psalms say God alone can do in commanding the sea.
options.note: Wind and sea obey Him, as the LORD stills the storm in Psalm 107; hence the disciples' awe.

options.text: That He has power to protect His disciples from danger.
options.note: True, but the deeper revelation is His divine identity as the One creation obeys.

options.text: That He was a skilled sailor who knew the lake.
options.note: He did not manage the boat; He commanded the elements with a word, a divine act.

options.text: That storms are not really dangerous.
options.note: The storm truly threatened to sink them; the point is Jesus' authority over it.

quiz.q: Why does Jesus ask the disciples, do you still have no faith?

options.text: Because their terror showed they did not yet trust the One present with them in the boat.
options.note: Mark 4:40; faith would rest in Jesus' presence and power even amid the storm.

options.text: Because they had woken Him from sleep.
options.note: Waking Him was not the failure; the issue was their fear that He did not care and could not help.

options.text: Because they lacked the skill to save the boat.
options.note: The rebuke concerned trust in Him, not their seamanship.

options.text: Because faith would have stopped the storm by itself.
options.note: It was Jesus, not their faith, that stilled the storm; He calls them to trust Him.

questions: Jesus warns us to examine what kind of soil our hearts are. Which soil best describes how you have been hearing God's word lately, and why?
The worries of life, the deceit of wealth, and the desire for other things can choke the word. Which of these thorns most threatens fruitfulness in your life right now?
The kingdom grows by God's power even while the farmer sleeps. How does this free you from thinking that God's work depends on your striving?
The disciples asked whether Jesus cared that they were perishing. When have you been tempted to think God was asleep or indifferent to your storm?
The disciples asked, who is this? How would truly grasping that the Lord of wind and wave is with you change the way you face your fears this week?

translationNotes.note: The words about seeing but not perceiving quote Isaiah 6:9-10; they describe the judicial hardening of those who persistently refuse, not a denial of mercy to any who would turn.
He swings the sickle because the harvest has come echoes Joel 3:13, tying the parable to God's final ingathering.
Silence, be still translates a strong command, literally be muzzled; Jesus addresses the sea as He addresses demons, treating the chaos as something to be subdued by His word.
